title: Half treble — the compromise stitch
subtitle: Taller than double crochet, shorter than treble, and quicker than either
excerpt: Half treble is the mid-height stitch — one yarn-over before inserting, three loops pulled through at once. Its slight angle and soft drape make it the best stitch for hats, cowls, and anything that needs to move with the wearer.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776 — the half treble as an intermediate height stitch. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Vol. 2 (1887) — half treble in border patterns.

glossaryTerms.definition: UK term for the mid-height crochet stitch: yarn over before inserting hook, pull up a loop, yarn over and pull through all three loops at once. US patterns call this half double crochet.

The loop formed by the yarn-over on entry that sits behind the two standard top loops of a half treble. Working into this loop instead of the top two creates a flat, smooth fabric called camel stitch or third-loop htr.

content.text: sits between double crochet and treble in height. One yarn-over before inserting, and the finish is a single pull-through all three loops at once rather than the two-stage pull-through of the treble. The resulting stitch has a slight forward lean and a softer, springier quality than either neighbour. US patterns call it half double crochet (hdc).
Chain 13. The turning chain for htr is ch 2. Some patterns count it as a stitch; others don't. This swatch counts it as a stitch so the edge stays tidy.
Row 1: ch 2 (counts as the first htr). Yarn over, then insert hook into the 3rd chain from the hook.
Yarn over and pull up a loop — three loops on the hook.
Yarn over and pull through all three loops at once. One htr made.
Work 1 htr in each chain across. At the end of the foundation chain you should have 12 htr including the ch-2. Turn.
Row 2: ch 2 (counts as first htr), skip the stitch directly below the ch-2. Work 1 htr in each stitch across. Finish with 1 htr into the top of the ch-2 from the previous row. 12 htr. Turn.

attrs.title: The third loop
attrs.body: Every htr has a hidden loop — called the third loop or back loop — formed by the yarn-over on entry. It sits directly behind the two standard top loops of the stitch. Working into this third loop instead of the usual top two creates camel stitch: a flat, smooth, woven-looking fabric with no visible ridges. Worth trying once you're comfortable with the basic htr.

content.text: When htr works better than dc or tr

Double crochet is denser and firmer; treble is taller and more open. Half treble is the middle choice for fabric that needs to move — hats, cowls, and the body of cardigans where treble would be too loose and double crochet too stiff. It also works well in ribbed cuffs and brim bands when worked in back-loop only.

items.symptom: Stitch count drifts after a few rows
items.cause: The ch-2 turning chain is inconsistently counted — sometimes as a stitch, sometimes not
items.fix: Check the pattern and pick one convention throughout. Mark the ch-2 with a stitch marker when it counts as a stitch so you can see clearly where the row starts.

items.cause: Three loops pulled through together can slip if the tension is loose
items.fix: Hold the working yarn with slightly more tension during the final pull-through. The three loops closing tightly creates the characteristic spring of the stitch.

items.symptom: A visible hole at the join of each row
items.cause: A gap forms between the ch-2 and the first stitch of the previous row when the turning chain counts as a stitch
items.fix: Skip the first stitch at the base of the ch-2. The ch-2 stands in for that stitch. Work into the second stitch of the row below.

content.text: The third-loop half treble (camel stitch) is the next level — working into the hidden loop changes the texture entirely. The herringbone half treble modifies the standard pull-through to create a diagonal woven surface. Both use the same entry move as the standard htr.
